title: Merge requires three passing checks

beats.say: On run fourteen eighty-one, the service and the model both say merge. Follow the three wires from the test runner, the scan service, and the review log to their copies in the model record. Which value changed on the way?

The scan. Its service value is true. The model copied false and still picked merge. The action matches the three passing service checks. Change the model’s scan field to true. Now its evidence matches too.

Try the shorter record. It supplies the test result and asks for manual review. Count what arrived. One of three fields is present, and its proposed action disagrees with the rule. These are deliberately faulty records.
Keep three scores. Count the fields, compare their Boolean values to their sources, then compare the action to the policy. We’ll use those scores when we compare prompts.

title: Where does the next step get its two?

beats.say: Where does a written step help? Give a decoder the beginning of a subtraction, six minus four equals. It runs its layers and proposes the digit two. Append that two to the prefix. The next prediction can read a subtotal that didn't exist on the first pass. That growing sequence is a scratchpad.

The subtotal came from the model. A wrong subtotal can carry forward, and a later step can correct it. A key and value cache reuses earlier projections. Each additional token still goes through the layers and attends to the retained context.
A native reasoning model can do that work behind a very short answer. Two replies of the same visible length can cost different amounts.

Merrill and Sabharwal studied what intermediate steps make possible in a specified transformer. Under their precision and normalization assumptions, polynomially many steps can express polynomial-time computation. Some separations rely on unproved complexity assumptions. Whether training actually found a useful procedure is something we can test on held-out problems.

title: What does a worked example teach?

beats.say: One prompt shows the fields we need. Another works through a separate release where the scan failed and explains why the answer is manual review. That second example teaches a step someone could repeat on a new case. Supplying solved examples like this is few-shot chain-of-thought prompting.
Asking for steps without any examples is zero-shot. To find out what the demonstration buys us, keep the target facts, policy and output fields fixed.

Wei and colleagues tried eight worked examples on grade-school math problems. With their PaLM model, accuracy rose from about eighteen percent to nearly fifty-seven. Kojima and colleagues showed that even a zero-shot request to think step by step could elicit intermediate steps. These experiments give us prompt variants to try on the release task.

The task matters. A June twenty twenty-five study on G P Q A found modest average gains for non-reasoning models. Reasoning models gained little and spent more time. A different study on nine pattern-based datasets found that asking for steps hurt performance across sixteen models.

On the same held-out releases, measure parse failures and missing checks separately. A template can fix the first while leaving the second untouched. Compare final actions, tokens and latency as well.

title: What can an operator inspect?

beats.say: What could you inspect to find that wrong scan? The decision record gives you a field to compare with the source. Asking a model for intermediate steps gives you generated text. A native reasoning model can spend internal tokens processing the request.
A provider may also return a summary describing that work. Each of those answers a different question. Neither a summary nor a written explanation establishes which internal steps caused the answer.

Suppose we set an eight-hundred-token output limit on a request to OpenAI's Responses API. Each internal reasoning token draws from that allowance. The counter reaches eight hundred while the decision record is still empty. Mark the response incomplete.

OpenAI's Responses API reports the token count and keeps the raw reasoning private. If the model supports summaries, you can request one. Check what your own endpoint returns before deciding what to log.

Turpin and colleagues changed features such as the order of the answer options. A model's prompted explanation could justify a choice without mentioning the feature that influenced it. That experiment studied prompted text. For a release audit, keep the inputs, validated fields, tool observations and actual outcome.
Limit who can access sensitive intermediate text and how long you keep it.

title: Five replies to one release request

beats.say: Here are five sampled replies to the same request. Read just the final action from each one. The first three use different words for merge. The fourth asks for manual review. The last asks to force a merge. Our list of allowed actions has no entry for that.
We sampled five paths, so each reply gets one seat, even the rejected one. Suppose a recommendation needs sixty percent support. Does merge qualify?

Yes. Three of five is sixty percent, exactly on the line. Now raise the requirement to eighty percent. The same replies fall one vote short, so the controller abstains. Manual review is a policy answer. An abstention means the vote didn't choose one.

Sampling paths and counting their final answers is called self-consistency. The most frequent answer can win a plurality with less than half the votes. Our stricter rule needs a unique winner and a finite numeric threshold above one half and at most one.

A boolean isn't a threshold. Empty batches, ties and batches with no valid votes all abstain. Check the response schema and match only an allowed final action. A rationale might say never merge and still contain the word merge.

Temperature and truncation affect which paths you sample. Copying one reply five times adds no independent evidence. Even separate draws can share a mistake. The vote selects a candidate for the same policy check we used on the release record.

title: What changes when each case gets five samples?

beats.say: For this trial, we’re back to a sixty percent minimum. Each release has five handwritten replies, so three votes for the same allowed action are enough. Look at the row where all five say merge. The expected action is manual review. Five votes repeat the same mistake. A failed scan would still block that release.

In the last row the first answer was right, but the vote abstains. Across all five cases the first reply gets two releases right with five samples. The vote gets three releases right with twenty-five samples. That raises accuracy from forty to sixty percent on these cases.

In a separate math experiment, Wang and colleagues sampled forty outputs per run. Their PaLM model went from fifty-six point five percent with greedy reasoning to seventy-four point four with self-consistency. The baseline belongs to this experiment.
Agreement can correlate with accuracy, but three votes out of five isn't a calibrated probability that an answer is correct.

For a service, compare both strategies on the same held-out requests. Count abstentions and invalid replies, repeat stochastic trials and measure unsafe approvals separately. With just five releases, either accuracy estimate could change substantially on a larger trial. You might run all five calls at once to save wall time.
You still pay to generate five replies, and longer replies can cost more even when the call count stays fixed.

title: Which answer does the next check need?

beats.say: This release changes authentication and logging. First identify the components and verify them against the diff. Pass that list to the next question. Authentication needs a security check. Logging needs a log-schema check. Drop logging from the first answer and watch what disappears downstream.
Solving dependent questions in order is called least-to-most prompting.

Suppose the security and performance reviewers can work separately. The combined release record now has two parents. A reviewer can send feedback and ask for a revision. Those joins and revisions are what a graph-of-thoughts controller adds. Retain both versions and score them. Feedback can make a previously correct answer worse.

While those reviewers work in parallel, both branches need their own active histories. A shared prefix cache can reuse the common prompt on a system that supports it. Each changed history still takes work.
When the next question depends on the previous answer, that wait is on the critical path. Measure the latency before deciding to put the workflow in an interactive service.

title: Four numbers leave room for different plans

beats.say: Read the four tiles from left to right. Six, four, five, seven. Use each exactly once with ordinary arithmetic to make twenty-four. The goal sounds simple because the answer is one number.
Choose six and four. Multiply them. Twenty-four takes their place. Look back at the tray. Five and seven are still loose. Has this move met both requirements?
The value is right, but two cards still have to be used. Keep alternatives, check each move, and track how much search remains. Let’s build that controller from this deal.

title: A written step gives the next step something to use

beats.say: A state records the values still available and the operation that produced them. One valid first move is six minus four, which leaves two, five, and seven.
Combine five and seven into twelve. The state now contains two and twelve. The two came from six and four. The twelve came from five and seven. We can use both subtotals in the next move.

Multiply two by twelve and the final state contains twenty-four. Each state has one continuation here. That makes this a linear path. A generated explanation can guide the next token, while the host still checks the arithmetic.

title: What survives the first move?

beats.say: Make two copies of the starting tray. On the left, choose six and four. On the right, leave those two alone and choose five and seven. Both trays started with the same four inputs.
On the left, multiply. Six times four gives twenty-four. Five and seven stay put. On the right, add. Five plus seven gives twelve. Six and four stay put. Which two originals are inside that twelve?

Read the two marks on the twelve. They name five and seven. Each branch stores its remaining values, its parent and the move it made. A controller can replay that move before it spends time searching below it.

title: Which next state belongs in the search?

beats.say: Two proposals claim to multiply six by four. The first lists only the product. The second also lists five and seven. Replay the move on the host’s own tray. Lift the six and the four. Put their product back. Which list describes everything still on the table?

Admit the second list. Twenty-four, five and seven are all still available. Both proposals got the product right. Only one preserved the untouched inputs. The host checks two available occurrences, an allowed operator, and exact fractions. Division needs a nonzero divisor.
A legal first move can still lead to a dead end.

Now add four and five, then add six and seven. Reverse the order of those two additions on the other path. Both leave nine and thirteen. Either way, the next move has the same two numbers to work with.
Keep one history for the pair and expand it once. The starting tray also counts toward the state budget.

In tree-of-thoughts, a model can propose and score the next moves. Here a small program enumerates every allowed pair and operation, so we can check the search against a known answer. The state budget bounds the number it examines. A service also needs limits on proposals, memory and elapsed time.

title: Which state gets expanded next?

beats.say: We have several states we could explore. The ones still waiting form the frontier. Watch the order here. A arrives first. B arrives second. Take from the front of a queue and A goes next. Applied at each depth, that rule gives us breadth-first search.
Push the same pair onto a stack, A first, then B. Which one comes off the top?
B comes off first. A is still waiting. If B leads to a dead end we can come back for A. Following the most recent choice first gives us depth-first search.

A beam changes the question. We score the proposals and keep a fixed number at this selection step. With room for one, the discarded sibling disappears from this run. Let's see what that costs on these two trays.

title: Which proposal does the beam keep?

beats.say: Suppose these are the two proposals at this fork. The scores are made up. The scorer likes seeing twenty-four already on the tray. That shortcut is a heuristic. It gives A ninety-five hundredths and B forty hundredths. The controller can keep just one. Which tray gets the next search?

A gets the slot. Turn B face down. Its score and its possible descendants are out of reach in this run. Try every legal continuation of A. The waiting count falls to zero after eighty-five distinct states. No solution from A. We have learned nothing about the discarded hand.

Start again at the fork. Both proposals are face up, and the slot is empty. Find the twelve in B's hand. It carries the five and seven. Keep the scores fixed and give the beam two places. Now we can explore B as well as A.
Six minus four leaves two. Two times twelve makes twenty-four. Trace it back and each input appears once. Widening the beam made that check possible and cost us another branch to examine.

title: Agreement and verification answer different questions

beats.say: Self-consistency samples several reasoning paths and votes on their extracted answers. It can help when different paths make different mistakes and converge on the same correct result.
In this fixture, three samples all say twenty-four, but each only multiplies six by four. Their agreement is high, while the original puzzle still has two unused numbers.
The host checks every operand and every operation in the winning expression. Agreement counts repeated answers. The checker tests the puzzle constraints. Shared mistakes can fool a vote.

title: What can a stopped search report?

beats.say: Give the original four-number puzzle a budget of one distinct state. Examining the starting tray spends that slot and leaves thirty-six states waiting. Now start from A's tray, twenty-four, five and seven, with that same one-state cap. It leaves eighteen waiting. We haven't found a solution. What status can we return for A?

Budget exhausted. The solver examined one tray. It adds a state to this queue only the first time it sees those values together, so the eighteen waiting states are all distinct and unexamined. In a queue that allows duplicates, skip already examined states before deciding whether any work remains. Time and tokens have separate budgets.

Run A again with exactly the same numbers and operations. This time lift the cap. Start the queue with A. Each point shows the number waiting after one more distinct state has been examined. At first, new moves arrive faster than the solver can inspect them.
Eventually we've examined eighty-five distinct states and the queue is empty. None reached a lone twenty-four. What can we say about this tray now?

No solution from this tray under these four operations. We can stop expanding A. The earlier capped run could only tell us to allow more work or report that the search was unfinished. A production controller also limits time, memory and the proposals it accepts at each step.

title: What changed between these two models?

beats.say: Give a model a new worked example and the prompt changes. Train on scored solutions and the parameters can change. OpenAI used reinforcement learning to train o one. DeepSeek's R one Zero began reinforcement learning without a preceding supervised fine-tuning stage.
DeepSeek observed it revisiting earlier steps and exploring alternatives. R one used both supervised and reinforcement stages.

Think back to the puzzle checker. A program can score a math answer, run a code test or check a proof. That score can serve as a reward during training. An algorithm such as G R P O uses rewards for sampled outputs to update the model.
Useful intermediate steps can emerge if they help earn the reward. Supervised training can also teach solutions from people or other models.

How should we spend a fixed compute budget? Snell and colleagues tried two ways to spend more of it at inference time on MATH problems. Their tuned PaLM two models could revise an answer or search with a verifier.

With matched compute budgets, the smaller model sometimes beat one with about fourteen times as many parameters. The result depended on problem difficulty and the balance between training and inference.

title: What did three passing tests establish?

beats.say: A function should double its input. Here is the candidate: double inputs up to three, and return zero above three. The test suite tries one, two and three. It gets two, four and six. All three tests pass. What will the same function return for four?

Zero. The caller expected eight. Passing the suite earned the reward for those three cases. The fourth case shows the gap in what the suite measured. A programmatic reward can encourage a shortcut. In a coding study, Anthropic observed this in deliberately vulnerable training environments.
Evaluate behavior such as agreeing with a user's false claim separately.

The release record gives us three other things we can actually check. Compare its scan field with the service when an explanation sounds convincing. Compare action errors and token usage when longer reasoning seems helpful.
If the response uses its output budget before producing a record, mark it incomplete. Each observation points to a different next step.

title: Which strategy fits the service?

beats.say: Each dot is one strategy on the same task. These are invented measurements. Farther left means faster. Higher means more correct answers. The service requires at least ninety percent accuracy and a p ninety-five latency of at most nine hundred milliseconds.
That's the time by which ninety-five percent of requests finish. Which dot meets both limits?

Vote five. It gets ninety-four percent correct at seven hundred forty milliseconds. Direct prompting and a single trace fall below the accuracy floor. Tree search reaches higher, but its eighteen hundred forty milliseconds misses the deadline.
Among eligible strategies, choose the fewest calls, then the lower p ninety-five to break a tie. Five calls can cost quite different amounts depending on the model and the tokens each call generates.
Keep every dot where it is. Change just the deadline to one hundred milliseconds. What qualifies now?

None. Even the fastest dot is at one hundred ninety. Report that no strategy meets the requirements. Also check the measurements before placing a dot. Infinite accuracy and negative latency would both pass a careless pair of comparisons.
Require a name, finite accuracy between zero and one, a finite positive latency and a positive integer call count. A missing field or a boolean call count fails validation.
With real data, compare native models and external controllers on the same held-out requests, including unsafe approvals, parse failures, abstentions and uncertainty.

Try a fresh comparison with the original limits. A pair of calls gets ninety-two percent correct at eight hundred thirty milliseconds. A five-call vote gets ninety-six percent at six hundred eighty milliseconds. Both qualify. Which would the service choose under its fewest-calls rule?
Choose the pair. Both clear the accuracy floor and the latency deadline. Two calls cost fewer requests than five. Token counts and prices would tell you the actual bill.

title: Match the reasoning method to the shape of the task

beats.say: Read the facts for this release. All three flags are available. Run the conjunction in code. A short factual question may need a single call. To derive checks from changed components, pass the verified component list into the next question.
Voting suits tasks with short canonical answers and useful sample diversity. Search suits tasks with legal partial states, a way to check moves, and alternatives worth revisiting.

Compare each method on held-out tasks with the same evaluator. Record correctness, abstention, cost, and latency. More intermediate text or a larger search tree earns its place only when the measured task needs it.

title: Four tiles, two threes and two eights

beats.say: Try four new tiles. There are two eights and two threes. The little letters tell the copies apart. Pair an eight with a three on each side. Both differences are five. Multiply the fives and you get twenty-five. We've spent all four tiles and missed by one.

Deal the same tiles again. This time divide the first eight by the first three. Keep eight thirds exactly. To make a small divisor, take that fraction away from the other three. Three is nine thirds, so the difference is one third. There's one untouched eight.
What operation between that eight and one third makes twenty-four?

Divide. Eight divided by one third is twenty-four. Read the four occurrence marks under that result. Each occurs once. Rounding eight thirds to two point six seven would lose the exact divisor that made this work.
Now suppose a proposed trace names eight A again for the last division. The numerical answer stays twenty-four. Would you accept that trace?

Reject it. Eight A was spent in the first division, and eight B is still on the table. Replace the repeated eight A with eight B. Now the exact arithmetic and the four occurrence checks pass. If a search hits its cap with an unexamined state still waiting, it can report that work remains.

title: Can this release merge?

beats.say: A new run, fourteen eighty-two. The deployed version is seventeen. The model recommends merging version eighteen. Tests passed and review is approved. Find the empty scan socket. Where can you get the missing value for this run?

Ask the scan service about run fourteen eighty-two. The model proposes a typed read. The runtime checks the run identifier and the caller’s read permission. Send that one request. Until an observation comes back, version seventeen stays deployed.

The reply says the scan failed. Put false in the scan socket. The model’s proposal still says merge. Apply the three-check rule. Manual review. Version seventeen stays deployed. Log the run, the observation and both actions together. The next lesson follows a function call from its schema to its result.
